versions.title: Drones: Flying Without a Pilot
versions.text:
A drone is a small flying toy. It has no pilot. A man on the ground flies it with a control.

Long ago, this was not so. Big planes had a pilot. He sat inside. That was the only way up.

Then makers made a new toy. It had no seat at all. A man on the ground used a control to make it fly. This was new.

At first, it could fly just a bit. It often crashed down. But it showed the idea could work.

Now drones do many jobs. Some take fun shots from the sky. Some drop small boxes at our door. Some help find lost hikers. This idea opened up the sky to us all.

versions.title: Drones: Flying Without a Pilot
versions.text:
A drone is formally known as an unmanned aerial vehicle. It is an aircraft that flies without any pilot aboard. A human operator or onboard computer controls it instead from the ground. For most of aviation history, every aircraft required a pilot seated inside to steer it through the sky.

That began changing in the twentieth century. Engineers built increasingly capable remote-controlled aircraft. Early military versions were used mainly for scouting and target practice. They often crashed after only a few flights. These unmanned aircraft gradually became more reliable. Battery technology, cameras, and radio controls all improved considerably.

By the early twenty-first century, drones had become small and affordable. They were widely available to ordinary consumers, not just military groups. Hobbyists could now buy a camera-equipped drone. It could capture stunning aerial photos and videos. Once, this was possible only with expensive helicopters.

Today, drones serve countless purposes beyond simple photography. Farmers use them to inspect crops across large fields. Delivery companies test dropping packages at doorsteps. Rescue teams deploy them to search remote wilderness for missing hikers. This expansion from crude military scouts to versatile everyday tools shows how fast drone technology has changed modern life.

Drones now also inspect bridges, power lines, and tall buildings, jobs once dangerous for human workers to climb. Filmmakers use them to capture sweeping aerial shots once possible only with a full helicopter crew. As safety regulations continue to develop, drones seem likely to take on even more tasks in the years ahead.

Many countries now require drone owners to register larger drones and follow rules about where and how high they may fly. These regulations help protect airplanes, keep people's privacy safe, and prevent accidents. Hobby pilots also race small drones through obstacle courses at high speed, turning the technology into an exciting new sport enjoyed by fans around the world.

Farmers use drones to inspect crops across large fields, delivery companies test dropping small packages at doorsteps, and rescue teams rely on drones to search for lost hikers deep in the woods. This remarkable improvement shows how quickly drone technology has changed modern life.

checklist: Explains that drones, formally called unmanned aerial vehicles, began as crude military tools used for scouting and target practice
Describes how improving battery, camera, and control technology made drones small, affordable, and widely available to consumers
Explains that many countries now require registration and rules to protect airplanes, privacy, and public safety
HIGH.modelAnswer: A drone, formally known as an unmanned aerial vehicle, began in the twentieth century as a crude military tool used mainly for scouting and target practice, often crashing after only a handful of flights. As battery technology, cameras, and radio controls steadily improved, these unmanned aircraft became far more reliable. By the early twenty-first century, drones had become small, affordable, and widely available to ordinary consumers, who could now capture stunning aerial photographs once possible only with expensive helicopters. Today, drones are remarkably versatile, serving purposes from inspecting bridges and crops to delivering packages and searching for lost hikers. Because of this rapid growth, many countries now require owners to register larger drones and follow regulations about where and how high they may fly, protecting airplanes, privacy, and public safety as this technology continues to expand into new areas of modern life.
